payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the image show the original visual content rendered in a pencil-drawn style?
node.criteria: Pass if the image visibly represents its content as a pencil drawing; fail if there is sufficient evidence that no pencil-drawing transformation has occurred; unknown if the image or its style cannot be assessed reliably. Partial evidence of a pencil-drawn style is progress, not completion.
node.binding: Compare the supplied image with the requested transformation: assess whether its visual content is rendered in a pencil-drawn style. Do not require a particular pencil technique.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them with muted, grainy, pencil-like shading and outlines.

The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting, but renders them with muted, mostly monochrome tones and visible fine grain and sketch-like shading consistent with a pencil-drawn style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them in a muted, textured pencil-drawing style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them with muted, grainy, pencil-like shading and softened outlines, consistent with a pencil-drawn style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting but renders them with muted, desaturated tones and visible fine grain and sketch-like shading consistent with a pencil-drawn style.

fulfillment: The node’s completion criterion is too permissive and unstable: several traces call the image complete based on muted tones, grain, and sketch-like shading, while another identifies substantial photographic color, shading, and detail and correctly treats it as partial. In the edited image, the scene is desaturated and textured, but retains photographic-looking forms and lighting; those style cues alone do not establish that the whole image reads as a completed pencil drawing. Tighten the whole-image criterion to distinguish a pencil-like filter/progress from a convincing drawing, and require explicit evidence addressing residual photographic appearance before marking complete. Keep support evidence for progress separate from the whole-image completion judgment, and preserve the existing partial/unknown distinctions. The transport failure is an evidence-availability failure, not negative visual evidence; keep it unresolved rather than treating it as a fail. Repeated variation and high confidence do not settle the visual ambiguity, so make the criterion more discriminative rather than forcing the reference label.
s3: The binding already asks for a whole-image judgment, but its contrast with “only limited pencil-style treatment” can let broad desaturation, grain, and softened edges count as completion. Make the decision criterion distinguish a pencil drawing from a photograph with a pencil-like filter: assess whether the scene’s forms, shading, and surface appearance consistently read as drawn, and explicitly weigh residual photographic lighting, texture, and detail rather than treating muted color or grain as sufficient. Keep evidence of visible stylistic progress separate from the completion judgment; do not require monochrome or a particular technique. Preserve unresolved for genuinely insufficient visual evidence. The transport failure is a call/evidence-availability problem, not a visual fail; repeated high-confidence disagreement is a criterion-calibration signal, not grounds to force a label.
s2: The node is a support check for any visible progress, so do not turn it into a whole-image completion test or require the scene to convincingly read as a finished drawing; that belongs in the downstream fulfillment criterion. The comparison shows broad desaturation and grain, with softened, sketch-like treatment across the food and surrounding objects, but substantial photographic forms and lighting remain. Make the support criterion distinguish genuine requested stylistic progress from color change or texture alone, and require evidence of drawing-like treatment in the depicted content rather than treating muted tones or grain by themselves as sufficient. Keep partial progress eligible to pass this support check, while leaving completion to the aggregate rubric. Preserve unknown when visual evidence is insufficient; transport or dependency failures are evidence-availability issues, not visual failures. Repeated high-confidence variation signals criterion ambiguity, not grounds to force a label or prescribe a particular output.
